entries.06cef57e4709e6fbadc5cc08b79d7c0c2b82b902: <div sID="gen9669" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="18" osisID="Job.18" sID="Job.18"/> <div eID="gen9669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9670" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9671" type="x-p"/> In this chapter Bildad makes a second assault upon Job. In his first discourse (<reference osisRef="Job.8.1-Job.8.22">ch. viii.</reference>) he had given him encouragement to hope that all should yet be well with him. But here there is not a word of that; he has grown more peevish, and is so far from being convinced by Job's reasonings that he is but more exasperated. I. He sharply reproves Job as haughty and passionate, and obstinate in his opinion, <reference osisRef="Job.18.1-Job.18.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. He enlarges upon the doctrine he had before maintained, concerning the miser of wicked people and the ruin that attends them, <reference osisRef="Job.18.5-Job.18.21">ver. 5-21</reference>. In this he seems, all along, to have an eye to Job's complaints of the miserable condition he was in, that he was in the dark, bewildered, ensnared, terrified, and hastening out of the world. "This," says Bildad, "is the condition of a wicked man; and therefore thou art one."
entries.ad76766dc980af52ef8f93e4f01387e84a8ccc16: <div eID="gen9671" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9670" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Second Address of Eliphaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9672" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then answered Bildad the Shuhite, and said, 2 How long <hi type="italic">will it be ere</hi> ye make an end of words? mark, and afterwards we will speak. <hi type="super">3</hi> Wherefore are we counted as beasts, <hi type="italic">and</hi> reputed vile in your sight? <hi type="super">4</hi> He teareth himself in his anger: shall the earth be forsaken for thee? and shall the rock be removed out of his place? <div eID="gen9672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9673" type="x-p"/> Bildad here shoots his arrows, even bitter words, against poor Job, little thinking that, though he was a wise and good man, in this instance he was serving Satan's design in adding to Job's affliction. <div eID="gen9673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9674" type="x-p"/> I. He charges him with idle endless talk, as Eliphaz had done (<reference osisRef="Job.15.2-Job.15.3">ch. xv. 2, 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">How long will it be ere you make an end of words?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.18.2">v. 2</reference>. Here he reflects, not only upon Job himself, but either upon all the managers of the conference (thinking perhaps that Eliphaz and Zophar did not speak so closely to the purpose as they might have done) or upon some that were present, who possibly took part with Job, and put in a word now and then in his favour, though it be not recorded. Bildad was weary of hearing others speak, and impatient till it came to his turn, which cannot be observed to any man's praise, for we ought to be swift to hear and slow to speak. It is common for contenders to monopolize the reputation of wisdom, and then to insist upon it as their privilege to be dictators. How unbecoming this conduct is in others every one can see; but few that are guilty of it can see it in themselves. Time was when Job had the last word in all debates (<reference osisRef="Job.29.22">ch. xxix. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">After my words they spoke not again.</hi> Then he was in power and prosperity; but now that he was impoverished and brought low he could scarcely be allowed to speak at all, and every thing he said was as much vilified as formerly it had been magnified. <hi type="italic">Wisdom</hi> therefore (as the world goes) <hi type="italic">is good with an inheritance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.11">Eccl. vii. 11</reference>); for <hi type="italic">the poor man's wisdom is despised,</hi> and, because he is poor, <hi type="italic">his words are not heard,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.16">Eccl. ix. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen9674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9675" type="x-p"/> II. With a regardlessness of what was said to him, intimated in that, <hi type="italic">Mark, and afterwards we will speak.</hi> And it is to no purpose to speak, though what is said be ever so much to the purpose, if those to whom it is addressed will not mark and observe it. Let the <hi type="italic">ear be opened to hear as the learned,</hi> and then the tongues of the learned will do good service (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa. l. 4</reference>) and not otherwise. It is an encouragement to those that speak of the things of God to see the hearers attentive. <div eID="gen9675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9676" type="x-p"/> III. With a haughty contempt and disdain of his friends and of that which they offered (<reference osisRef="Job.18.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore are we counted as beasts?</hi> This was invidious. Job had indeed called them <hi type="italic">mockers,</hi> had represented them both as unwise and as unkind, wanting both in the reason and tenderness of men, but he did not count them beasts; yet Bildad so represents the matter, 1. Because his high spirit resented what Job had said as if it had been the greatest affront imaginable. Proud men are apt to think themselves slighted more than really they are. 2. Because his hot spirit was willing to find a pretence to be hard upon Job. Those that incline to be severe upon others will have it thought that others have first been so upon them. <div eID="gen9676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9677" type="x-p"/> IV. With outrageous passion: <hi type="italic">He teareth himself in his anger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.18.4">v. 4</reference>. Herein he seems to reflect upon what Job had said (<reference osisRef="Job.13.14">ch. xiii. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore did I take my flesh in my teeth?</hi> "It is thy own fault," says Bildad. Or he reflected upon what he said <reference osisRef="Job.16.9">ch. xvi. 9</reference>, where he seemed to charge it upon God, or, as some think, upon Eliphaz: <hi type="italic">He teareth me in his wrath.</hi> "No," says Bildad; "thou alone shalt bear it." <hi type="italic">He teareth himself in his anger.</hi> Note, Anger is a sin that is its own punishment. Fretful passionate people tear and torment themselves. <hi type="italic">He teareth his soul</hi> (so the word is); every sin wounds the soul, tears that, wrongs that (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.36">Prov. viii. 36</reference>), unbridled passion particularly. <div eID="gen9677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9678" type="x-p"/> V. With a proud and arrogant expectation to give law even to Providence itself: "<hi type="italic">Shall the earth be forsaken for thee?</hi> Surely not; there is no reason for that, that the course of nature should be changed and the settled rules of government violated to gratify the humour of one man. Job, dost thou think the world cannot stand without thee; but that, if thou art ruined, all the world is ruined and forsaken with thee?" Some make it a reproof of Job's justification of himself, falsely insinuating that either Job was a wicked man or we must deny a Providence and suppose that God has forsaken the earth and the rock of ages is removed. It is rather a just reproof of his passionate complaints. When we quarrel with the events of Providence we forget that, whatever befals us, it is, 1. According to the eternal purpose and counsel of God. 2. According to the written word. Thus it is written that in the world we must have tribulation, that, since we sin daily, we must expect to smart for it; and, 3. According to the usual way and custom, the track of Providence, nothing but what is common to men; and to expect that God's counsels should change, his method alter, and his word fail, to please us, is as absurd and unreasonable as to think <hi type="italic">the earth should be forsaken for us and the rock removed out of its place.</hi>
entries.a3301b8b9499f201c5bd178068641f352e180824: <div eID="gen9678" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Miserable Condition of the Wicked. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9679" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Yea, the light of the wicked shall be put out, and the spark of his fire shall not shine. <hi type="super">6</hi> The light shall be dark in his tabernacle, and his candle shall be put out with him. <hi type="super">7</hi> The steps of his strength shall be straitened, and his own counsel shall cast him down. <hi type="super">8</hi> For he is cast into a net by his own feet, and he walketh upon a snare. <hi type="super">9</hi> The gin shall take <hi type="italic">him</hi> by the heel, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the robber shall prevail against him. <hi type="super">10</hi> The snare <hi type="italic">is</hi> laid for him in the ground, and a trap for him in the way. <div eID="gen9679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9680" type="x-p"/> The rest of Bildad's discourse is entirely taken up in an elegant description of the miserable condition of a wicked man, in which there is a great deal of certain truth, and which will be of excellent use if duly considered—that a sinful condition is a sad condition, and that iniquity will be men's ruin if they do not repent of it. But it is not true that all wicked people are visibly and openly made thus miserable in this world; nor is it true that all who are brought into great distress and trouble in this world are <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> to be deemed and adjudged wicked men, when no other proof appears against them; and therefore, though Bildad thought the application of it to Job was easy, yet it was not safe nor just. In these verses we have, <div eID="gen9680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9681" type="x-p"/> I. The destruction of the wicked foreseen and foretold, under the similitude of darkness (<reference osisRef="Job.18.5-Job.18.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yea, the light of the wicked shall be put out.</hi> Even his <hi type="italic">light,</hi> the best and brightest part of him, shall be put out; even that which he rejoiced in shall fail him. Or the <hi type="italic">yea</hi> may refer to Job's complaints of the great distress he was in and the darkness he should shortly make his bed in. "Yea," says Bildad, "So it is; thou art clouded, and straitened, and made miserable, and no better could be expected; for <hi type="italic">the light of the wicked shall be put out,</hi> and therefore thine shall." Observe here, 1. The wicked may have some light for a while, some pleasure, some joy, some hope within, as well as wealth, and honour, and power without. But his light is but a spark (<reference osisRef="Job.18.5">v. 5</reference>), a little thing and soon extinguished. It is but a candle (<reference osisRef="Job.18.6">v. 6</reference>), wasting, and burning down, and easily blown out. It is not the light of the Lord (that is sun-light), but the <hi type="italic">light of his own fire</hi> and <hi type="italic">sparks of his own kindling,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.11">Isa. l. 11</reference>. 2. His light will certainly be put out at length, quite put out, so that not the least spark of it shall remain with which to kindle another fire. Even while he is in his tabernacle, while he is in the body, which is the tabernacle of the soul (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2 Cor. v. 1</reference>), the light shall be dark; he shall have no true solid comfort, no joy that is satisfying, no hope that is supporting. Even <hi type="italic">the light that is in him is darkness;</hi> and <hi type="italic">how great is that darkness!</hi> But, when he is put out of this tabernacle by death, <hi type="italic">his candle shall be put out with him.</hi> The period of his life will be the final period of all his days and will turn all his hopes into endless despair. <hi type="italic">When a wicked man dies his expectation shall perish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.7">Prov. xi. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">He shall lie down in sorrow.</hi> <div eID="gen9681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9682" type="x-p"/> II. The preparatives for that destruction represented under the similitude of a beast or bird caught in a snare, or a malefactor arrested and taken into custody in order to his punishment, <reference osisRef="Job.18.7-Job.18.10">v. 7-10</reference>. 1. Satan is preparing for his destruction. He is <hi type="italic">the robber that shall prevail against him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.18.9">v. 9</reference>); for, as he was a murderer, so he was a robber, from the beginning. He, as the tempter, lays snares for sinners in the way, wherever they go, and he shall prevail. If he make them sinful like himself, he will make them miserable like himself. He <hi type="italic">hunts for the precious life.</hi> 2. He is himself preparing for his own destruction by going on in sin, and so <hi type="italic">treasuring up wrath against the day of wrath.</hi> God gives him up, as he deserves and desires, to his own counsels, and then <hi type="italic">his own counsels cast him down,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.18.7">v. 7</reference>. His sinful projects and pursuits bring him into mischief. He is <hi type="italic">cast into a net by his own feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.18.8">v. 8</reference>), runs upon his own destruction, is <hi type="italic">snared in the work of his own hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Ps. ix. 16</reference>); his <hi type="italic">own tongue falls upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.64.8">Ps. lxiv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare.</hi> 3. God is preparing for his destruction. The sinner by his sin is preparing the fuel and then God by his wrath is preparing the fire. See here, (1.) How the sinner is infatuated, to run himself into the snare; and whom God will destroy he infatuates. (2.) How he is embarrassed: <hi type="italic">The steps of his strength,</hi> his mighty designs and efforts, <hi type="italic">shall be straitened,</hi> so that he shall not compass what he intended; and the more he strives to extricate himself the more will he be entangled. Evil men wax worse and worse. (3.) How he is secured and kept from escaping the judgments of God that are in pursuit of him. <hi type="italic">The gin shall take him by the heel.</hi> He can no more escape the divine wrath that is in pursuit of him than a man, so held, can flee from the pursuer. God <hi type="italic">knows how to reserve the wicked for the day of judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.9">2 Pet. ii. 9</reference>.
entries.7f90e9ed3b50de9b377c9a81064b45ba19293f6a: <div eID="gen9682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9683" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Terrors shall make him afraid on every side, and shall drive him to his feet. <hi type="super">12</hi> His strength shall be hungerbitten, and destruction <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> ready at his side. 13 It shall devour the strength of his skin: <hi type="italic">even</hi> the firstborn of death shall devour his strength. <hi type="super">14</hi> His confidence shall be rooted out of his tabernacle, and it shall bring him to the king of terrors. <hi type="super">15</hi> It shall dwell in his tabernacle, because <hi type="italic">it is</hi> none of his: brimstone shall be scattered upon his habitation. <hi type="super">16</hi> His roots shall be dried up beneath, and above shall his branch be cut off. <hi type="super">17</hi> His remembrance shall perish from the earth, and he shall have no name in the street. <hi type="super">18</hi> He shall be driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the world. <hi type="super">19</hi> He shall neither have son nor nephew among his people, nor any remaining in his dwellings. <hi type="super">20</hi> They that come after <hi type="italic">him</hi> shall be astonied at his day, as they that went before were affrighted. 21 Surely such <hi type="italic">are</hi> the dwellings of the wicked, and this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the place <hi type="italic">of him that</hi> knoweth not God. <div eID="gen9683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9684" type="x-p"/> Bildad here describes the destruction itself which wicked people are reserved for in the other world, and which, in some degree, often seizes them in this world. Come, and see what a miserable condition the sinner is in when his day comes to fall. <div eID="gen9684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9685" type="x-p"/> I. See him disheartened and weakened by continual terrors arising from the sense of his own guilt and the dread of God's wrath (<reference osisRef="Job.18.11-Job.18.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Terror shall make him afraid on every side.</hi> The terrors of his own conscience shall haunt him, so that he shall never be easy. Wherever he goes, these shall follow him; which way soever he looks, these shall stare him in the face. It will make him tremble to see himself fought against by the whole creation, to see Heaven frowning on him, hell gaping for him, and earth sick of him. He that carries his own accuser, and his own tormentor, always in his bosom, cannot but be afraid on every side. This will drive him to his feet, like the malefactor, who, being conscious of his own guilt, takes to his heels and <hi type="italic">flees when none pursues,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Prov. xxviii. 1</reference>. But his feet will do him no service; they are fast in the snare, <reference osisRef="Job.18.9">v. 9</reference>. The sinner may as soon overpower the divine omnipotence as flee from the divine omniscience, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.2-Amos.9.3">Amos ix. 2, 3</reference>. No marvel that the sinner is dispirited and distracted with fear, for, 1. He sees his ruin approaching: <hi type="italic">Destruction shall be ready at his side,</hi> to seize him whenever justice gives the word, so that he is <hi type="italic">brought into desolation in a moment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.19">Ps. lxxiii. 19</reference>. 2. He feels himself utterly unable to grapple with it, either to escape it or to bear up under it. That which he relied upon as <hi type="italic">his strength</hi> (his wealth, power, pomp, friends, and the hardiness of his own spirit) <hi type="italic">shall</hi> fail him in the time of need, and <hi type="italic">be hunger-bitten,</hi> that is, it shall do him no more service than a famished man, pining away for hunger, would do in work or war. The case being thus with him, no marvel that he is a terror to himself. Note, The way of sin is a way of fear, and leads to everlasting confusion, of which the present terrors of an impure and unpacified conscience are earnests, as they were to Cain and Judas. <div eID="gen9685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9686" type="x-p"/> II. See him devoured and swallowed up by a miserable death; and miserable indeed a wicked man's death is, how secure and jovial soever his life was. 1. See him dying, arrested by <hi type="italic">the first-born of death</hi> (some disease, or some stroke that has in it a more than ordinary resemblance of death itself; <hi type="italic">so great a death,</hi> as it is called, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.10">2 Cor. i. 10</reference>, a messenger of death that has in it an uncommon strength and terror), weakened by the harbingers of death, which <hi type="italic">devour the strength of his skin,</hi> that is, it shall bring rottenness into his bones and consume them. <hi type="italic">His confidence shall then be rooted out of his tabernacle</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.18.14">v. 14</reference>), that is, all that he trusted to for his support shall be taken from him, and he shall have nothing to rely upon, no, not his own tabernacle. His own soul was his confidence, but that shall be rooted out of the tabernacle of the body, as a tree that cumbered the ground. "Thy soul shall be required of thee." 2. See him dead, and see his case then with an eye of faith. (1.) He is then brought to <hi type="italic">the king of terrors.</hi> He was surrounded with terrors while he lived (<reference osisRef="Job.18.11">v. 11</reference>), and death was the king of all those terrors; they fought against the sinner in death's name, for it is by reason of death that sinners are <hi type="italic">all their lifetime subject to bondage</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.15">Heb. ii. 15</reference>), and at length they will be brought to that which they so long feared, as a captive to the conqueror. Death is terrible to nature; our Saviour himself prayed, <hi type="italic">Father, save me from this hour.</hi> But to the wicked it is in a special manner <hi type="italic">the king of terrors,</hi> both as it is a period to that life in which they placed their happiness and a passage to that life where they will find their endless misery. How happy then are the saints, and how much indebted to the Lord Jesus, by whom death is so far abolished, and the property of it altered, that this king of terrors becomes a friend and servant! (2.) He is then <hi type="italic">driven from the light into darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.18.18">v. 18</reference>), from the light of this world, and his prosperous condition in it, into darkness, the darkness of the grave, the darkness of hell, into utter darkness, never to see light (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.19">Ps. xlix. 19</reference>), not the least gleam, nor any hopes of it. (3.) He is then <hi type="italic">chased out of the world,</hi> hurried and dragged away by the messengers of death, sorely against his will, chased as Adam out of paradise, for the world is his paradise. It intimates that he would fain stay here; he is loth to depart, but go he must; all the world is weary of him, and therefore chases him out, as glad to get rid of him. This is death to a wicked man. <div eID="gen9686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9687" type="x-p"/> III. See his family sunk and cut off, <reference osisRef="Job.18.15">v. 15</reference>. The wrath and curse of God light and lie, not only upon his head and heart, but upon his house too, to consume it with the <hi type="italic">timber and stones thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.5.4">Zech. v. 4</reference>. Death itself shall dwell in his tabernacle, and, having expelled him, shall take possession of his house, to the terror and destruction of all that he leaves behind. Even the dwelling shall be ruined for the sake of its owner: <hi type="italic">Brimstone shall be scattered upon his habitation,</hi> rained upon it as upon Sodom, to the destruction of which this seems to have reference. Some think he here upbraids Job with the burning of his sheep and servants with fire from heaven. The reason is here given why his tabernacle is thus marked for ruin: <hi type="italic">Because it is none of his;</hi> that is, it was unjustly got, and kept, from the rightful owner, and therefore let him not expect either the comfort or the continuance of it. His children shall perish, either with him or after him, <reference osisRef="Job.18.16">v. 16</reference>. So that, <hi type="italic">his roots being</hi> in his own person <hi type="italic">dried up beneath, above his branch</hi> (every child of his family) <hi type="italic">shall be cut off.</hi> Thus the houses of Jeroboam, Baasha, and Ahab, were cut off; none that descended from them were left alive. Those who take root in the earth may expect it will thus be dried up; but, if we be rooted in Christ, even our leaf shall not wither, much less shall our branch be cut off. Those who consult the true honour of their family, and the welfare of its branches, will be afraid of withering it by sin. The extirpation of the sinner's family is mentioned again (<reference osisRef="Job.18.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall neither have son nor nephew,</hi> child nor grandchild, to enjoy his estate and bear up his name, <hi type="italic">nor</hi> shall there be <hi type="italic">any remaining in his dwelling</hi> akin to him. Sin entails a curse upon posterity, and the iniquity of the fathers is often visited upon the children. Herein, also, it is probable that Bildad reflects upon the death of Job's children and servants, as a further proof of his being a wicked man; whereas all that are written childless are not thereby written graceless; there is a name <hi type="italic">better than that of sons and daughters.</hi> <div eID="gen9687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9688" type="x-p"/> IV. See his memory buried with him, or made odious; he shall either be forgotten or spoken of with dishonour (<reference osisRef="Job.18.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">His remembrance shall perish from the earth;</hi> and, if it perish thence, it perishes wholly, for it was never written in heaven, as the names of the saints are, <reference osisRef="Luke.10.20">Luke x. 20</reference>. All his honour shall be laid and lost in the dust, or stained with perpetual infamy, so that <hi type="italic">he shall have no name in the street,</hi> departing without being desired. Thus the judgments of God follow him, after death, in this world, as an indication of the misery his soul is in after death, and an earnest of that everlasting shame and contempt to which he shall rise in the great day. <hi type="italic">The memory of the just is blessed, but the name of the wicked shall rot,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.10.7">Prov. x. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen9688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9689" type="x-p"/> V. See a universal amazement at his fall, <reference osisRef="Job.18.20">v. 20</reference>. Those that see it are affrighted, so sudden is the change, so dreadful the execution, so threatening to all about him: and those that come after, and hear the report of it, are astonished at it; their ears are made to tingle, and their hearts to tremble, and they cry out, <hi type="italic">Lord, how terrible art thou in thy judgments!</hi> A place or person utterly ruined is said to be <hi type="italic">made an astonishment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.28.37 2Chr.7.21">Deut. xxviii. 37; 2 Chron. vii. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.9 Jer.25.18">Jer. xxv. 9, 18</reference>. Horrible sins bring strange punishments. <div eID="gen9689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9690" type="x-p"/> VI. See all this averred as the unanimous sense of the patriarchal age, grounded upon their knowledge of God and their many observations of his providence (<reference osisRef="Job.18.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Surely such are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place</hi> (this the condition) <hi type="italic">of him that knows not God!</hi> See here what is the beginning, and what is the end, of the wickedness of this wicked world. 1. The beginning of it is ignorance of God, and it is a wilful ignorance, for there is that to be known of him which is sufficient to leave them for ever inexcusable. They know not God, and then they commit all iniquity. Pharaoh knows not the Lord, and therefore will not obey his voice. 2. The end of it, and that is utter destruction. <hi type="italic">Such,</hi> so miserable, <hi type="italic">are the dwellings of the wicked.</hi> Vengeance will be taken of those that <hi type="italic">know not God,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.8">2 Thess. i. 8</reference>. For those whom he has not honour from he will get himself honour upon. Let us therefore stand in awe and not sin, for it will certainly be bitterness in the latter end.  <chapter eID="Job.18"/> <div eID="gen9690" type="x-p"/>

entries.fa5d71589b68649ad883fda5f723ccca69f85fad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4826"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <div sID="gen7051" type="x-p"/> SECOND SERIES.<div eID="gen7051" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.18.1-Job.18.21">Job 18:1-21</reference>. Reply of Bildad.</title> <div sID="gen7052" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4826"/><hi type="bold">2. ye--</hi>the other two friends of Job, whom Bildad charges with having spoken mere "words," that is, empty speeches; opposed to "mark," that is, come to reason, consider the question intelligently; and then let us speak. <div eID="gen7052" type="x-p"/>
entries.34ba820b47479f6c4b8a56605c370e3364c1c646: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4827"/><div sID="gen7053" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4827"/><hi type="bold">3. beasts--</hi>alluding to what Job said (<reference osisRef="Job.12.7">Job 12:7</reference>; so <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Is 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen7053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7054" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vile--</hi>rather from a Hebrew root, "to stop up." "Stubborn," answering to the stupidity implied in the parallel first clause [Umbreit]. Why should we give occasion by your empty speeches for our being mutually reputed, in the sight of Job and one another, as unintelligent? (<reference osisRef="Job.17.4">Job 17:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.17.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen7054" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfcd01067008b8b04d73e6f331c9b899b8238773: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4828"/><div sID="gen7055" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4828"/>4. Rather, turning to Job, "thou that tearest thyself in anger" (<reference osisRef="Job.5.2">Job 5:2</reference>).<div eID="gen7055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be forsaken?--</hi>become desolate. He alludes here to Job's words as to the "rock," crumbling away (<reference osisRef="Job.14.18">Job 14:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.14.19">19</reference>); but in a different application. He says bitterly "for thee." Wert thou not punished as thou art, and as thou art unwilling to bear, the eternal order of the universe would be disturbed and the earth become desolate through unavenged wickedness [Umbreit]. Bildad takes it for granted Job is a great sinner (<reference osisRef="Job.8.3-Job.8.6">Job 8:3-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.5">Is 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.6">6</reference>). "Shall that which stands fast as a rock be removed for your special accommodation?" <div eID="gen7056" type="x-p"/>
entries.e851b5eacea3680c42832572ab48545d99741115: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4829"/><div sID="gen7057" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4829"/>5. That (<reference osisRef="Job.18.4">Job 18:4</reference>) cannot be. The decree of God is unalterable, the light (prosperity) of the wicked shall at length be put out.<div eID="gen7057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his fire--</hi>alluding to Arabian hospitality, which prided itself on welcoming the stranger to the fire in the tent, and even lit fires to direct him to it. The ungodly shall be deprived of the means to show hospitality. His dwelling shall be dark and desolate! <div eID="gen7058" type="x-p"/>
entries.1935cf4a798655355a56958b06b3b390bffc85cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4830"/><div sID="gen7059" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4830"/><hi type="bold">6. candle--</hi>the lamp which in the East is usually fastened to the ceiling. Oil abounds in those regions, and the lamp was kept burning all night, as now in Egypt, where the poorest would rather dispense with food than the night lamp (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.28">Psa 18:28</reference>). To put out the lamp was an image of utter desolation. <div eID="gen7059" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5eaba0d39c405f717d7ebb34d82d0ff5c56073d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4831"/><div sID="gen7060" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4831"/><hi type="bold">7. steps of his strength--</hi>Hebrew, for "His strong steps." A firm step marks health. To be straitened in steps is to be no longer able to move about at will (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.12">Pr 4:12</reference>).<div eID="gen7060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7061" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his own counsel--</hi>Plans shall be the means of his fall (<reference osisRef="Job.5.13">Job 5:13</reference>). <div eID="gen7061" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d541246c7280956a282572909b038fa5ec283e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4832"/><div sID="gen7062" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4832"/><hi type="bold">8. he walketh upon--</hi>rather, "he lets himself go into the net" [Umbreit]. If the English Version be retained, then understand "snare" to be the pitfall, covered over with branches and earth, which when walked upon give way (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.15">Psa 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.8">35:8</reference>). <div eID="gen7062" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f02260ddcb0bbc87611612d1a1f195ef1bfa339: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4833"/><div sID="gen7063" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4833"/><hi type="bold">9. robber--</hi>rather answering to "gin" in the parallel clause, "the noose shall hold him fast" [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7063" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9c739c379ccfa0344b6555966696b71e9c552d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4834"/><div sID="gen7064" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4834"/><hi type="bold">11. Terrors--</hi>often mentioned in this book (<reference osisRef="Job.18.14">Job 18:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.17">24:17</reference>; &c.). The terrors excited through an evil conscience are here personified. "Magor-missabib" (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.3">Jr 20:3</reference>).<div eID="gen7064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drive ... to his feet--</hi>rather, "shall pursue" (literally, "scatter," <reference osisRef="Hab.3.14">Ha 3:14</reference>) him close "at his heels" (literally, "immediately after his feet," <reference osisRef="Hab.3.5">Ha 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.42">1Sa 25:42</reference>; Hebrew). The image is that of a pursuing conqueror who scatters the enemy [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7065" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd04650321f793c6a72b27c23fb915e594890771: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4835"/><div sID="gen7066" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4835"/>12. The Hebrew is brief and bold, "his strength is hungry."<div eID="gen7066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destruction--</hi>that is, a great calamity (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.27">Pr 1:27</reference>).<div eID="gen7067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7068" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ready at his side--</hi>close at hand to destroy him (<reference osisRef="Prov.19.29">Pr 19:29</reference>). <div eID="gen7068" type="x-p"/>
entries.700483f66eb8aa4d9328318797111eb3041b39b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4836"/><div sID="gen7069" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4836"/>13. Umbreit has "he" for "it," that is, "in the rage of hunger he shall devour his own body"; or, "his own children" (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.10">La 4:10</reference>). Rather, "destruction" from <reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference> is nominative to "devour."<div eID="gen7069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strength--</hi>rather, "members" (literally, the "branches" of a tree).<div eID="gen7070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the first-born of death--</hi>a personification full of poetical horror. The first-born son held the chief place (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.3">Ge 49:3</reference>); so here the chiefest (most deadly) disease that death has ever engendered (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.30">Is 14:30</reference>; "first-born of the poor"--the poorest). The Arabs call fever, "daughter of death." <div eID="gen7071" type="x-p"/>
entries.8734a8fdc21c6c1f2917295180cfd43b39d31d12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4837"/><div sID="gen7072" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4837"/><hi type="bold">14. confidence--</hi>all that the father trusted in for domestic happiness, children, fortune, &c., referring to Job's losses.<div eID="gen7072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rooted out--</hi>suddenly torn away, it shall bring--that is, he shall be brought; or, as Umbreit better has, "Thou (God) shalt bring him slowly." The Hebrew expresses, "to stride slowly and solemnly." The godless has a fearful death for long before his eyes, and is at last taken by it. Alluding to Job's case. The King of terrors, not like the heathen Pluto, the tabled ruler of the dead, but Death, with all its terrors to the ungodly, personified. <div eID="gen7073" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3e5e173bf2f1281ac46fa0cafefbf9ca121b419: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4838"/><div sID="gen7074" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4838"/><hi type="bold">15. It--</hi>"Terror" shall haunt, &c., and not as Umbreit, "another," which the last clause of the verse disproves.<div eID="gen7074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">none of his--</hi>It is his no longer.<div eID="gen7075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brimstone--</hi>probably comparing the calamity of Job by the "fire of God" (<reference osisRef="Job.1.16">Job 1:16</reference>) to the destruction of guilty Sodom by fire and brimstone (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.24">Ge 19:24</reference>). <div eID="gen7076" type="x-p"/>
entries.00b92cc9b79d62965ecb16ce6360b619fc607736: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4839"/><div sID="gen7077" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4839"/><hi type="bold">16. Roots--</hi>himself.<div eID="gen7077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branch--</hi>his children (<reference osisRef="Job.8.12">Job 8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.30">15:30</reference>; Mal 4:1). <div eID="gen7078" type="x-p"/>
entries.6548b2452bd0bba41dae57c3c95682799983688b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4840"/><div sID="gen7079" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4840"/><hi type="bold">17. street--</hi>Men shall not speak of him in meeting in the highways; rather, "in the field" or "meadow"; the shepherds shall no more mention his name--a picture from nomadic life [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7079" type="x-p"/>
entries.05ba14cac8288cfa598784ec9205af4d7631227a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4841"/><div sID="gen7080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4841"/><hi type="bold">18. light ... darkness--</hi>existence--nonexistence. <div eID="gen7080" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae5a2472478312b6e761693e31a79e82b2ce82b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4842"/><div sID="gen7081" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4842"/><hi type="bold">19. nephew--</hi>(so <reference osisRef="Isa.14.22">Is 14:22</reference>). But it is translated "grandson" (<reference osisRef="Gen.21.23">Ge 21:23</reference>); translate "kinsman." <div eID="gen7081" type="x-p"/>
entries.812d72932fb1cd5468827d1e4d94fad35078fe80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4843"/><div sID="gen7082" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4843"/><hi type="bold">20. after ... before--</hi>rather, "those in the West--those in the East"; that is, all people; literally, "those behind--those before"; for Orientals in geography turn with their faces to the east (not to the north as we), and back to the west; so that before--east; behind--north (so <reference osisRef="Zech.14.8">Zec 14:8</reference>).<div eID="gen7082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day--</hi>of ruin (Ob 12).<div eID="gen7083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7084" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">affrighted--</hi>seized with terror (<reference osisRef="Job.21.6">Job 21:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.8">Is 13:8</reference>). <div eID="gen7084" type="x-p"/>
entries.09a3c7ba3a7b5643175f26972ba27f014c695469: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4844"/><div sID="gen7085" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4844"/>21. (<reference osisRef="Job.8.22">Job 8:22</reference>, Margin). <chapter eID="Job.18"/>

entries.a33c9ae0f30b38e6b53c461d10cbef0ac8078ef1: <div eID="gen16695" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16696" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16697" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16697" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16696" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16698" type="x-p"/> Bildad, in a speech of passionate invective, accuses Job of impatience and impiety, <reference osisRef="Job.18.1-Job.18.4">Job 18:1-4</reference>; shows the fearful end of the wicked and their posterity; and apparently applies the whole to Job, whom he threatens with the most ruinous end, vv. 5-21. <div eID="gen16698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16699" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen16699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16700" type="x-p"/> Then answered Bildad - The following analysis of this speech, by Mr. Heath, is judicious: "Bildad, irritated to the last degree that Job should treat their advice with so much contempt, is no longer able to keep his passions within the bounds of decency. He proceeds to downright abuse; and finding little attention given by Job to his arguments, he tries to terrify him into a compliance. To that end he draws a yet more terrible picture of the final end of wicked men than any yet preceding, throwing in all the circumstances of Job's calamities, that he might plainly perceive the resemblance, and at the same time insinuating that he had much worse still to expect, unless he prevented it by a speedy change of behavior. That it was the highest arrogance in him to suppose that he was of consequence enough to be the cause of altering the general rules of Providence, <reference osisRef="Job.18.4">Job 18:4</reference>. And that it was much more expedient for the good of the whole, that he, by his example, should deter others from treading in the same path of wickedness and folly;" <reference osisRef="Job.18.5-Job.18.7">Job 18:5-7</reference>.
entries.1afb1b2105c1bbecfb2545fcd4802868685d80b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16701" type="x-p"/> How long will it be ere ye make an end - It is difficult to say to whom this address is made: being in the plural number, it can hardly be supposed to mean Job only. It probably means all present; as if he had said, It is vain to talk with this man, and follow him through all his quibbles: take notice of this, and then let us all deliver our sentiments fully to him, without paying any regard to his self-vindications. It must be owned that this is the plan which Bildad followed; and he amply unburdens a mind that was laboring under the spirit of rancour and abuse. Instead of How long will it be ere ye make an end of words? Mr. Good translates: "How long will ye plant thorns (irritating, lacerating, wounding invectives) among words?" translating the unusual term קנצי kintsey, thorns, instead of bounds or limits. The word קנצי kintsey may be the Chaldee form for קצי kitsey, the נ nun being inserted by the Chaldeans for the sake of euphony, as is frequently done; and it may be considered as the contracted plural from קץ kats, a thorn, from קץ kats, to lacerate, rather than קץ kets, an end, from קצה katsah, to cut off. Schultens and others have contended that קנץ kanats, is an Arabic word, used also in Hebrew; that (Arabic) kanasa, signifies to hunt, to lay snares; and hence (Arabic) maknas, a snare: and that the words should be translated, "How long will you put captious snares in words?" But I prefer קנצי kintsey, as being the Chaldee form for קצי kitsey, whether it be considered as expressing limits or thorns; as the whole instance is formed after the Chaldee model, as is evident, not only in the word in question, but also in למלין lemillin, to words, the Chaldee plural instead of למלים lemillim, the Hebrew plural.
entries.6b16dc1e70254a328e26c8525403af0cf28d60a8: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16702" type="x-p"/> Counted as beasts - Thou treatest us as if we had neither reason nor understanding.
entries.77ef2f0390f8bc7791676ef0b5be94003083643c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16703" type="x-p"/> He teareth himself in his anger - Literally, Rending his own soul in his anger; as if he had said, Thou art a madman: thy fury has such a sway over thee that thou eatest thy own flesh. While thou treatest us as beasts, we see thee to be a furious maniac, destroying thy own life. <div eID="gen16703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16704" type="x-p"/> Shall the earth be forsaken for thee? - To say the least, afflictions are the common lot of men. Must God work a miracle in providence, in order to exempt thee from the operation of natural causes? Dost thou wish to engross all the attention and care of providence to thyself alone? What pride and insolence!
entries.f84eae4eee375ce3e709caf3c7d05bcce7bd238f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16705" type="x-p"/> The light of the wicked shall be put out - Some think it would be better to translate the original, "Let the light of the wicked be extinguished!" Thou art a bad man, and thou hast perverted the understanding which God hath given thee. Let that understanding, that abused gift, be taken away. From this verse to the end of the chapter is a continual invective against Job.
entries.6584702356a72a71ece7927149dbc24efa691017: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16706" type="x-p"/> The light shall be dark in his tabernacle - His property shall be destroyed, his house pillaged, and himself and his family come to an untimely end. <div eID="gen16706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16707" type="x-p"/> His candle shall be put out - He shall have no posterity.
entries.899ea74d0997fd3281a219f101fe923148d1aa81: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16708" type="x-p"/> The steps of his strength - Even in his greatest prosperity he shall be in straits and difficulties. <div eID="gen16708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16709" type="x-p"/> His own counsel - He shall be the dupe and the victim of his own airy, ambitious, and impious schemes.
entries.e6d3b3454d264b44b6e062641ee2d3948d9ff93a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16710" type="x-p"/> For he is cast into a net - His own conduct will infallibly bring him to ruin. He shall be like a wild beast taken in a net; the more he flounces in order to extricate himself, the more he shall be entangled. <div eID="gen16710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16711" type="x-p"/> He walketh upon a snare - He is continually walking on the meshes of a net, by which he must soon be entangled and overthrown.
entries.d2d0eaf9c3773cb30622fa3d5503e8830d0a7cf6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16712" type="x-p"/> The gin shall take him - Houbigant reads the tenth before the ninth verse, thus: "The snare is laid for him in the ground, and a trap for him in the way. The gin shall take him by the heel, and the robber shall prevail against him." From the beginning of the seventh verse to the end of the thirteenth there is an allusion to the various arts and methods practiced in hunting. 1. A number of persons extend themselves in a forest, and drive the game before them, still straitening the space from a broad base to a narrow point in form of a triangle, so that the farther they go the less room have they on the right and left, the hunters lining each side, while the drovers with their dogs are coming up behind. "The steps of his strength shall be straitened," <reference osisRef="Job.18.7">Job 18:7</reference>. 2. Nets, gins, and pitfalls, are laid or formed in different places, so that many are taken before they come to the point where the two lines close. "He is cast into a net, he walketh upon a snare - the trap is laid for him in the way - the snare in the ground," <reference osisRef="Job.18.8-Job.18.10">Job 18:8-10</reference>. 3. The howling of the dogs, with the shouts of the huntsmen, fill him with dismay, and cause him to run himself beyond his strength and out of breath. "Terrors shall make him afraid on every side, and shall drive him to his feet," <reference osisRef="Job.18.11">Job 18:11</reference>. 4. While spent with hunger and fatigue, he is entangled in the spread nets; and the huntsman either pierces him with an arrow or spear, or cuts the sinews of his legs, so that he is easily captured and destroyed. "The robbers shall prevail against him," <reference osisRef="Job.18.9">Job 18:9</reference>. "His strength is hunger-bitten, and destruction is ready at his side," <reference osisRef="Job.18.12">Job 18:12</reference>. This latter verse is thus paraphrased by the Chaldee: "Let his first-born son be famished; and affliction be prepared for his wife."
entries.8407a4b09f69268126936cd5e68052ca658ca492: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16713" type="x-p"/> It shall devour the strength of his skin - This may refer to the elephant, or to the rhinoceros, whose skin scarcely any dart can pierce: but in the case referred to above, the animal is taken in a pitfall, and then the first-born of death - a sudden and overwhelming stroke - deprives him of life. See the account of hunting the elephant in the East at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="Job.18.21">Job 18:21</reference> (note). The Chaldee has: "The strength of his skin shall devour his flesh; and the angel of death shall consume his children."
entries.801b5a25270eb6e19e90668f621c698bc89bf30b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16714" type="x-p"/> His confidence shall be rooted out - His dwelling-place, how well soever fortified, shah now he deemed utterly insecure. <div eID="gen16714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16715" type="x-p"/> And it shall bring him to the king of terrors - Or, as Mr. Good translates, "And dissolution shall invade him as a monarch." He shall be completely and finally overpowered. The phrase king of terrors has been generally thought to mean death; but it is not used in any such way in the text. For למלך בלהות lemelech ballahoth, to the king of destructions, one of De Rossi's MSS. has כמלך kemelech, "as a king;" and one, instead of בלהות ballahoth, with ו vau holem, to indicate the plural, terrors or destructions, has בלהות ballahuth, with ו vau shurek, which is singular, and signifies terror, destruction. So the Vulgate seems to have read, as it translates, Et calcet super eum, quasi rex, interitis; "And shall tread upon him as a king or destroyer. Or as a king who is determined utterly to destroy him." On this verse the bishop of Killala, Dr. Stock, says, "I am sorry to part with a beautiful phrase in our common version, the king of terrors, as descriptive of death; but there is no authority for it in the Hebrew text." It may however be stated that death has been denominated by similar epithets both among the Greeks and Romans. <div eID="gen16715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16716" type="x-p"/> So Virgil, Aen. vi., ver. 100. - <div eID="gen16716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16717" type="x-p"/> Quando hic inferni janua regi Dicitur. "The gates of the king of hell are reported to be here." <div eID="gen16717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16718" type="x-p"/> And Ovid, Metam. lib. v., ver. 356, 359. <div eID="gen16718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16719" type="x-p"/> Inde tremit tellus: et rex pavit ipse silentum. <div eID="gen16719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16720" type="x-p"/> Hanc metuens cladem, tenebrosa sede tyrannus Exierat. "Earth's inmost bowels quake, and nature groans; <div eID="gen16720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16721" type="x-p"/> His terrors reach the direful King of Hell. <div eID="gen16721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16722" type="x-p"/> Fearing this destruction, the tyrant left hisgloomy court." <div eID="gen16722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16723" type="x-p"/> And in Sophocles, (Oedip. Colon., ver. 1628, edit. Johnson). Εννυχιων αναξ, Αιδωνευ. "O Pluto, king of shades." <div eID="gen16723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16724" type="x-p"/> That is, the invisible demon, who dwells in darkness impenetrable. Old Coverdale translates: Very fearfulnesse shall bringe him to the kynge.
entries.245f92d09a415fa6d0f4fa187f48ac38df0d6a57: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16725" type="x-p"/> It shall dwell in his tabernacle - Desolation is here personified, and it is said that it shall be the inhabitant, its former owner being destroyed. Brimstone shall be scattered upon his habitation, so that, like Sodom and Gomorrah, it may be an everlasting monument of the Divine displeasure. In the Persian poet Saady, we find a couplet which contains a similar sentiment: - <div eID="gen16725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16726" type="x-p"/> Purdeh daree meekund dar keesri Keesar ankeboot <div eID="gen16726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16727" type="x-p"/> Boomee Noobat meezund ber kumbed Afraseeab. "The spider holds the veil in the palace of Caesar; <div eID="gen16727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16728" type="x-p"/> The owl stands sentinel on the watchtower of Afrasiab." <div eID="gen16728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16729" type="x-p"/> The palaces of those mighty kings are so desolate that the spider is the only chamberlain, and the owl the only sentinel. The web of the former is all that remains as a substitute for the costly veil furnished by the chamberlain in the palace of the Roman monarch; and the hooting of the latter is the only remaining substitute for the sound of drums and trumpets by which the guards were accustomed to be relieved at the watchtower of the Persian king. The word (Persic) Keesur, the same as kaisar or Caesar, is the term which the Asiatics always use when they designate the Roman emperor. Afrasiab was an ancient king who invaded and conquered Persia about seven hundred years before the Christian era. After having reigned twelve years, he was defeated and slain by Zalzer and his son, the famous Rustem. The present reigning family of Constantinople claim descent from this ancient monarch. <div eID="gen16729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16730" type="x-p"/> Brimstone shall be scattered upon his habitation - This may either refer to the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, as has already been intimated, or to an ancient custom of fumigating houses with brimstone, in order to purify them from defilement. Pliny says, Hist. Nat., lib. xxxv., c. 15, speaking of the uses of sulphur, Habet et in religionibus locum ad expiandas suffitu domos; which Dr. Holland paraphrases thus: "Moreover brimstone is employed ceremoniously in hallowing of houses; for many are of opinion that the perfume and burning thereof will keep out all enchantments; yea, and drive away foul fiends and evil sprites that do haunt a place." <div eID="gen16730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16731" type="x-p"/> Ovid refers to the same, De Arte. Am., lib. ii. ver. 329. <div eID="gen16731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16732" type="x-p"/> Et veniat, quae lustret anus lectumque locumque: <div eID="gen16732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16733" type="x-p"/> Praeferat et tremula sulphur et ova manu. <div eID="gen16733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16734" type="x-p"/> This alludes to the ceremony of purifying the bed or place in which a sick person was confined; an old woman or nurse was the operator, and eggs and sulphur were the instruments of purification. On this and other methods of purgation see an excellent note in Servius on these words of Virgil, Aen. vi., ver. 740. - <div eID="gen16734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16735" type="x-p"/> Aliae panduntur inanes <div eID="gen16735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16736" type="x-p"/> Suspensae ad ventos: aliis sub gurgite vasto <div eID="gen16736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16737" type="x-p"/> Infectum eluitur scelus, aut exuritur igni. "For this are various penances subjoin'd; <div eID="gen16737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16738" type="x-p"/> And some are hung to bleach upon the wind; <div eID="gen16738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16739" type="x-p"/> Some plunged in waters, others, plunged in fires." <div eID="gen16739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16740" type="x-p"/> Unde etiam, says Servius, in sacris Liberi omnibus tres sunt istae purgationes: nam aut taeda purgantur et sulphure, aut aqua abluuntur, aut aere ventilantur. "These three kinds of purgation are used in the rites of Bacchus: they are purged by flame and sulphur, or washed in water, or ventilated by the winds." <div eID="gen16740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16741" type="x-p"/> But it is most likely that Bildad, in his usual uncharitable manner, alludes to the destruction of Job's property and family by winds and fire: for the Fire of God fell from heaven and burnt up the sheep and the servants, and Consumed them; and a great wind, probably the sulphureous suffocating simoom, smote the four corners of the house, where Job's children were feasting, and killed them; see <reference osisRef="Job.1.16">Job 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.1.19">Job 1:19</reference>.
entries.3f4fc4965a0127acbd72e78d8d075a62af3a5d62: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16742" type="x-p"/> His roots shall be dried up - his branch be cut off - He shall be as utterly destroyed, both in himself, his posterity, and his property, as a tree is whose branches are all lopped off, and whose every root is cut away.
entries.ec975c98f65a39bb019fabe376ddc21c528e895a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16743" type="x-p"/> His remembrance shall perish - He shall have none to survive him, to continue his name among men. <div eID="gen16743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16744" type="x-p"/> No name in the street - He shall never be a man of reputation; after his demise, none shall talk of his fame.
entries.8b5c055f7faf91c800e8953618d87468cb008c25: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16745" type="x-p"/> He shall be driven from light - He shall be taken off by a violent death. <div eID="gen16745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16746" type="x-p"/> And chased out of the world - The wicked is Driven Away in his iniquity. This shows his reluctance to depart from life.
entries.6161ec94b18039c091c8a5f7368b71bfd1a8d59c: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16747" type="x-p"/> He shall neither have son nor nephew - Coverdale, following the Vulgate, translates thus: He shal neither have children ner kynss folk among his people, no ner eny posterite in his countrie: yonge and olde shal be astonyshed at his death.
entries.b41ce698aee910fdfaa2be49ae8ddfa54eb5f3d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16748" type="x-p"/> They that come after him - The young shall be struck with astonishment when they hear the relation of the judgments of God upon this wicked man. As they that went before. The aged who were his contemporaries, and who saw the judgments that fell on him, were affrighted, אחזו שער achazu saar, seized with horror - were horrified; or, as Mr. Good has well expressed it, were panic-struck.
entries.bec3822b6a93d1a69acfc1c06f5713919d93fbdc: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16749" type="x-p"/> Such are the dwellings - This is the common lot of the wicked; and it shall be particularly the case with him who knoweth not God, that is Job, for it is evident he alludes to him. Poor Job! hard was thy lot, severe were thy sufferings. On the elephant hunt to which I have referred, <reference osisRef="Job.18.13">Job 18:13</reference>, I shall borrow the following account extracted from Mr. Cordiner's History of Ceylon, by Mr. Good: - "We have a curious description of the elephant hunt, which is pursued in a manner not essentially different from the preceding, except that the snares are pallisadoed with the strongest possible stakes, instead of being netted, and still farther fortified by interlacings. They are numerous, but connected together; every snare or inclosure growing gradually narrower, and opening into each other by a gate or two that will only admit the entrance of a single animal at a time. "The wood in which elephants are known to abound is first surrounded, excepting at the end where the foremost and widest inclosure is situated, with fires placed on moveable pedestals, which in every direction are drawn closer and closer, and, aided by loud and perpetual shouts, drive the animals forward till they enter into the outer snare. After which the same process is continued, and they are driven by fear into a second, into a third, and into a fourth; till at length the elephants become so much sub-divided, that by the aid of cordage fastened carefully round their limbs, and the management of decoy elephants, they are easily capable of being led away one by one, and tamed. A single hunt thus conducted will sometimes occupy not less than two months of unremitting labor; and the entrance of the elephants into the snares is regarded as an amusement or sport of the highest character, and as such is attended by all the principal families of the country." Account of Ceylon, p. 218-226.  <chapter eID="Job.18"/> <div eID="gen16749" type="x-p"/>

entries.f8f37a3af06fc0ee37df385fa51fa1946f80cbc3: <reference osisRef="Job.18.1-Job.3.1">Job 18:1-3   1</reference>  Then began Bildad the Shuhite, and said:   2  How long will ye hunt for words?! <div eID="gen7599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7600" type="x-p"/> Attend, and afterwards we will speak.   3  Wherefore are we accounted as beasts, <div eID="gen7600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7601" type="x-p"/> And narrow-minded in your eyes? <div eID="gen7601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7602" type="x-p"/> Job’s speeches are long, and certainly are a trial of patience to the three, and the heaviest trial to Bildad, whose turn now comes on, because he is at pains throughout to be brief. Hence the reproach of endless babbling with which he begins here, as at <reference osisRef="Job.8.2">Job 8:2</reference>, when he at last has an opportunity of speaking; in connection with which it must, however, not be forgotten that Job also, <reference osisRef="Job.16.3">Job 16:3</reference>, satirically calls upon them to cease. He is indeed more entitled than his opponents to the entreaty not to weary him with long speeches. The question, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.18.2">Job 18:2</reference></hi>, if קנצי six derived from קץ, furnishes no sense, unless perhaps it is, with Ralbag, explained: how long do you make close upon close in order, when you seem to have come to an end, to begin continually anew? For to give the thought: how long do you make no end of speaking, it must have been לא עד־אנה, as the lxx (μέχρι τίνος ου ̓ παύσῃ:) involuntarily inserts the negative. And what should the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. mean by this rendering? The form קנצי = קצּי would not cause doubt; for though קצּים does not occur elsewhere in the Old Testament, it is nevertheless sufficient that it is good Aramaic (קצּין), and that another Hebr. plural, as קצי, קצוי, קצוות, would have been hardly in accordance with the usage of the language. But the plural would not be suitable here generally, the over-delicate explanation of Ralbag perhaps excepted. Since the book of Job abounds in Arabisms, and in Arabic <hi type="italic">qanaṣa</hi> (as synon. of <hi type="italic">ṣâd</hi>) signifies <hi type="italic">venari, venando capere,</hi> and <hi type="italic">qanṣun</hi> (<hi type="italic">maqnaṣun</hi>) <hi type="italic">cassis, rete venatorium;</hi> since, further, שׂים קנצים (comp. שׂים ארב, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.7">Jer 9:7</reference>) is an incontrovertible reading, and all the difficulties in connection with the reference to קץ lying in the עד־אנה for עד־אנה לא and in the plur. vanish, we translate with Castell., Schultens, J. D. Mich., and most modern expositors: how long (here not different from <reference osisRef="Job.8.2">Job 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.2">Job 19:2</reference>) will ye lay snares (construction, as also by the other rendering, like <reference osisRef="Job.24.5">Job 24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.16">Job 36:16</reference>, according to Ges. §116, 1) for words; which, however, is not equivalent to hunt for words in order to contradict, but in order to talk on continually.<note placement="foot">In post-bibl. Hebrew, קנצים has become common in the signification, proofs, arguments, as e.g., a Karaitic poet says, ויחוד שׁמך בקנצים הקימותי, the oneness of thy name have I upheld with proofs; vid., Pinsker, <hi type="italic">Likute Kadmoniot. Zur Gesch. des Karaismus und der karâischen Literatur</hi>, 1860, S. קסו.</note> <div eID="gen7602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7603" type="x-p"/> Job is the person addressed, for Bildad agrees with the two others. It is remarkable, however, that he addresses Job with “you.” Some say that he thinks of Job as one of a number; Ewald observes that the controversy becomes more wide and general; and Schlottm. conjectures that Bildad fixes his eye on individuals of his hearers, on whose countenances he believed he saw a certain inclination to side with Job. This conjecture we will leave to itself; but the remark which Schlottm. also makes, that Bildad regards Job as a type of a whole class, is correct, only one must also add, this address in the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. is a reply to Job’s sarcasm by a similar one. As Job has told the friends that they act as if they were mankind in general, and all wisdom were concentrated in them, so Bildad has taken it amiss that Job connects himself with the whole of the truly upright, righteous, and pure; and he addresses him in the plural, because he, the unit, has puffed himself up as such a collective whole. This wrangler - he means - with such a train behind him, cannot accomplish anything: Oh that you would understand (הבין, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">Job 42:3</reference>, not causative, as <reference osisRef="Job.6.24">Job 6:24</reference>), i.e., come to your senses, and afterward we will speak, i.e., it is only then possible to walk in the way of understanding. That is not now possible, when he, as one who plays the part of their many, treats them, the three who are agreed in opposition to him, as totally void of understanding, and each one of them unwise, in expressions like <reference osisRef="Job.17.4">Job 17:4</reference>, Job 17:10. Looking to <reference osisRef="Ps.49.13">Psa 49:13</reference>, 21, one might be tempted to regard נטמינוּ (on the vowel <hi type="italic">î</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">ê</hi>, vid., Ges. §75, rem. 7) as an interchange of consonants from נדמינו: be silent, make an end, ye <hi type="italic">profligati;</hi> but the supposition of this interchange of consonants would be arbitrary. On the other hand, there is no suitable thought in “why are we accounted unclean?” (Vulg. <hi type="italic">sorduimus</hi>), from טמה = טמא, <reference osisRef="Lev.11.43">Lev 11:43</reference> (Ges. §75, vi.); the complaint would have no right connection, except it were a very slight one, with Job 17:9. On the contrary, if we suppose a verb טמה in the signification <hi type="italic">opplere, obturare,</hi> which is peculiar to this consonant-combination in the whole range of the Semitic languages (comp. א־טם, Arab. <hi type="italic">'ṭm , obstruere,</hi> Aram. טמּם, טמטם, Arab. <hi type="italic">ṭmm ,</hi> e.g., Talm.: transgression stoppeth up, מטמטמת, man’s heart), and after which this טמה has been explained by the Jewish expositors (Raschi: נחשׁבנו טמומים), and is interpreted by סתם (Parchon: נסתמה דעתנו), we gain a sense which corresponds both with previous reproaches of Job and the parallelism, and we decide in its favour with the majority of modern expositors. With the interrogative Wherefore, Bildad appeals to Job’s conscience. These invectives proceed from an impassioned self-delusion towards the truth, which he wards off from himself, but cannot however alter.
entries.360bd963d9b413765b679a3cbb584ee9984d62a3: <reference osisRef="Job.18.4-Job.7.4">Job 18:4-7   4</reference>  Thou art he who teareth himself in his anger: <div eID="gen7603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7604" type="x-p"/> Shall the earth become desolate for thy sake, <div eID="gen7604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7605" type="x-p"/> And a rock remove from its place?   5  Notwithstanding, the light of the wicked shall be put out, <div eID="gen7605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7606" type="x-p"/> And the glow of his fire shineth not;   6  The light becometh dark in his tent, <div eID="gen7606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7607" type="x-p"/> And his lamp above him is extinguished;   7  His vigorous steps are straitened, <div eID="gen7607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7608" type="x-p"/> And his own counsel casteth him down. <div eID="gen7608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7609" type="x-p"/> The meaning of the strophe is this: Dost thou imagine that, by thy vehement conduct, by which thou art become enraged against thyself, thou canst effect any change in the established divine order of the world? It is a divine law, that sufferings are the punishment of sin; thou canst no more alter this, than that at thy command, or for thy sake, the earth, which is appointed to be the habitation of man (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.18">Isa 45:18</reference>), will become desolate (<hi type="italic">tê‛âzab</hi> with the tone drawn back, according to Ges. §29, 3, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, Arab. with similar signification in intrans. Kal <hi type="italic">t‛azibu</hi>), or a rock remove from its place (on יעתּק, vid., <reference osisRef="Job.14.18">Job 14:18</reference>). Bildad here lays to Job’s charge what Job, in <reference osisRef="Job.16.9">Job 16:9</reference>, has said of God’s anger, that it tears him: he himself tears himself in his rage at the inevitable lot under which he ought penitently to bow. The address, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.18.4">Job 18:4</reference></hi>, as <hi type="italic">apud Arabes ubique fere</hi> (Schult.), is put objectively (not: Oh thou, who); comp. what is said on כּלּם, <reference osisRef="Job.17.10">Job 17:10</reference>, which is influenced by the same syntactic custom. The lxx transl. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.18.4">Job 18:4</reference></hi>: Why! will Hades be tenantless if thou diest (ἐὰν σὺ ἀποθάνῃς)? after which Rosenm. explains: <hi type="italic">tuâ causâ h. e. te cadente.</hi> But that ought to be הבמוּתך. The peopling of the earth is only an example of the arrangements of divine omnipotence and wisdom, the continuance of which is exalted over the human power of volition, and does not in the least yield to human self-will, as (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.18.4">Job 18:4</reference></hi>) the rock is an example, and at the same time an emblem, of what God has fixed and rendered immoveable. That of which he here treats as fixed by God is the law of retribution. However much Job may rage, this law is and remains the unavoidable power that rules over the evil-doer.
entries.a2747b0022a9017d6628d63acd82c13b850c5ab5: <reference osisRef="Job.18.8-Job.11.8">Job 18:8-11   8</reference>  For he is driven into the net by his own feet, <div eID="gen7609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7610" type="x-p"/> And he walketh over a snare.   9  The trap holdeth his heel fast, <div eID="gen7610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7611" type="x-p"/> The noose bindeth him. 10  His snare lieth hidden in the earth, <div eID="gen7611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7612" type="x-p"/> His nets upon the path; 11  Terrors affright him on every side, <div eID="gen7612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7613" type="x-p"/> And scare him at every step. <div eID="gen7613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7614" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Pual</hi> שׁלּח signifies not merely to be betrayed into, but driven into, like the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.30.12">Job 30:12</reference>, to drive away, and as it is to be translated in the similar passage in the song of Deborah, Jdg 5:15 : “And as Issachar, Barak was driven (i.e., with desire for fighting) behind him down into the valley (the place of meeting under Mount Tabor);” בּרגליו, which there signifies, according to Jdg 4:10; Jdg 8:5, ”upon his feet = close behind him,” is here intended of the intermediate cause: by his own feet he is hurried into the net, i.e., against his will, and yet with his own feet he runs into destruction. The same thing is said in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.18.8">Job 18:8</reference></hi>; the way on which he complacently wanders up and down (which the <hi type="italic">Hithp.</hi> signifies here) is שׂבכה, lattice-work, here a snare (Arab. <hi type="italic">schabacah</hi>, a net, from שׂבך, <hi type="italic">schabaca</hi>, to intertwine, weave), and consequently will suddenly break in and bring him to ruin. This fact of delivering himself over to destruction is established in apocopated <hi type="italic">futt</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Job.18.9">Job 18:9</reference>) used as <hi type="italic">praes.,</hi> and without the voluntative signification in accordance with the poetic licence: a trap catches a heel (poetic brevity for: the trap catches his heel), a noose seizes upon him, עליו (but with the accompanying notion of overpowering him, which the translation “bind” is intended to express). Such is the meaning of צמּים here, which is not <hi type="italic">plur.,</hi> but <hi type="italic">sing.,</hi> from צמם (Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍmm</hi>), to tie, and it unites in itself the meanings of snare-layer (<reference osisRef="Job.5.5">Job 5:5</reference>) and of snare; the form (as אבּיר, אדּיר) corresponds more to the former, but does not, however, exclude the latter, as תּנּין and לפּיד (λαμπάς) show. <div eID="gen7614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7615" type="x-p"/> The continuation in <reference osisRef="Job.18.10">Job 18:10</reference> of the figure of the fowler affirms that that issue of his life (<reference osisRef="Job.18.9">Job 18:9</reference>) has been preparing long beforehand; the prosperity of the evil-doer from the beginning tends towards ruin. Instead of חבלו we have the pointing חבלו, as it would be in Arab. in a similar sense <hi type="italic">hhabluhu</hi> (from <hi type="italic">hhabl</hi>, a cord, a net). The nearer destruction is now to him, the stronger is the hold which his foreboding has over him, since, as <reference osisRef="Job.18.11">Job 18:11</reference> adds, terrible thoughts (בּלּהות) and terrible apparitions fill him with dismay, and haunt him, following upon his feet. לרגליו, close behind him, as <reference osisRef="Gen.30.30">Gen 30:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.42">1Sa 25:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa 41:2</reference>; Hab 3:5. The best authorized pointing of the verb is והפיצהוּ, with <hi type="italic">Segol</hi> (Ges. §104, 2, <hi type="italic">c</hi>), <hi type="italic">Chateph-Segol,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Kibbutz</hi>. Except in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.14">Hab 3:14</reference>, where the prophet includes himself with his people, הפיץ, <hi type="italic">diffundere, dissipare</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.37.11">Job 37:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.11">Job 40:11</reference>), never has a person as its obj. elsewhere. It would also probably not be used, but for the idea that the spectres of terror pursue him at every step, and are now here, now there, and his person is as it were multiplied.
entries.fee032b1ccf4885789d68a5531144e853ee14bf3: <reference osisRef="Job.18.12-Job.15.12">Job 18:12-15 12</reference>  His calamity looketh hunger-bitten, <div eID="gen7615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7616" type="x-p"/> And misfortune is ready for his fall. 13  It devoureth the members of his skin; <div eID="gen7616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7617" type="x-p"/> The first-born of death devoureth his members. 14  That in which he trusted is torn away out of his tent, <div eID="gen7617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7618" type="x-p"/> And he must march on to the king of terrors. 15  Beings strange to him dwell in his tent; <div eID="gen7618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7619" type="x-p"/> Brimstone is strewn over his habitation. <div eID="gen7619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7620" type="x-p"/> The description of the actual and total destruction of the evil-doer now begins with יהי (as <reference osisRef="Job.24.14">Job 24:14</reference>, after the manner of the voluntative forms already used in <reference osisRef="Job.24.9">Job 24:9</reference>). Step by step it traces his course to the total destruction, which leaves no trace of him, but still bears evident marks of being the fulfilment of the curse pronounced upon him. In opposition to this explanation, Targ., Raschi, and others, explain אנו according to <reference osisRef="Gen.49.3">Gen 49:3</reference> : the son of his manhood’s strength becomes hungry, which sounds comical rather than tragic; another Targ. transl.: he becomes hungry in his mourning, which is indeed inadmissible, because the signif. <hi type="italic">planctus</hi>, <hi type="italic">luctus</hi>, belongs to the derivatives of אנה, אנן, but not to און. But even the translation recently adopted by Ew., Stick., and Schlottm., “his strength becomes hungry,” is unsatisfactory; for it is in itself no misfortune to be hungry, and רעב does not in itself signify “exhausted with hunger.” It is also an odd metaphor, that strength becomes hungry; we would then rather read with Reiske, רעב באנו, <hi type="italic">famelicus in media potentia sua</hi>. But as און signifies strength (<reference osisRef="Job.18.7">Job 18:7</reference>), so און (root אן, to breathe and pant) signifies both wickedness and evil (the latter either as evil = calamity, or as <hi type="italic">anhelitus</hi>, sorrow, Arab. <hi type="italic">ain</hi>); and the thought that his (i.e., appointed to the evil-doer) calamity is hungry to swallow him up (Syr., Hirz., Hahn, and others), suits the parallelism perfectly: "and misfortune stands ready for his fall."<note placement="foot">If רעב elsewhere corresponds to the Arabic <hi type="italic">rugb</hi>, to be voraciously hungry, the Arab. <hi type="italic">ra‛b</hi>, to be paralyzed with fright, might correspond to it in the present passage: "from all sides spectres alarm him (בעתהו from בעת = Arab. <hi type="italic">bgt</hi>, to fall suddenly upon any one; or better: = <hi type="italic">b‛ṯ</hi>, to hunt up, excitare, to cause to rise, to fill with alarm) and urge him forward, seizing on his heels; then his strength becomes a paralyzing fright (רעב), and destruction is ready to overwhelm him." The <hi type="italic">ro‛b</hi> (רעב, thus in Damascus) or <hi type="italic">ra‛b</hi> (רעב, thus in Hauran and among the Beduins) is a state of mind which only occurs among us in a lower degree, but among the Arabs it is worthy of note as a psychological fact.
